doc.title: Paul Shaffer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 24, 2023

title: 'Cast Your Fate to the Wind' and Vince Guaraldi
summary: They discuss versions of 'Cast Your Fate to the Wind', Sounds Orchestral, Guaraldi's original and the key of A flat.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You’ve been very generous with your time, Paul, and I wanted to mention just a couple of things in wrapping up. First of all I wanted to thank you for one of your World’s Most Dangerous Band recordings because you chose “Cast Your Fate to the Wind” and “Yeh Yeh.”
Yes. Well they’re right in my, you know you and I obviously same reference points.
Yes. I can remember, this is not that uncommon but sometimes you hear the tunes, the cover versions of tunes first. When I heard “Cast Your Fate to the Wind” it was some © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-
nameless thing like some nameless orchestra covering it, and so I always thought that was it.

Well if I may, because I remember this and was alive then. It was way before your time, but whatever it was, ’64 maybe, the hit version was this orchestral thing you’re referring to. A nameless, you know a studio orchestra that they called Sounds Orchestral. That was the hit. To me, you’re right, that was the hit. The composer was Vince Guaraldi, the great jazz pianist from San Francisco who wrote the score to the Peanuts stuff on TV. But he didn’t have a hit on it. His version is interesting, a little more jazzy. It’s got a jazz section that I don’t think Sounds Orchestral used.

Sounds Orchestral was a British, you know, British arranger who made up a name, Sounds Orchestral, and went into the studio. But to me that’s the version. And I’ve learned it since I did “Shaggy” you may remember, I think, participated on that record. He transformed it too, did a marvelous job. But when I do have a little symphony show that I do once in a while when I can, and I do the Sounds Orchestral arrangement of that and I had a guy write all that piano stuff. I was able to, in my slow, and I can play all those licks now note for note.
I love it. And I think I noticed that on Vince’s recordings he did it in A flat and he also did the Charlie Brown iconic thing in A flat. Pardon?
Yeah. I said he must like the flats I guess.
